Adult Tarek (Alburnus tarichi), the endemic cyprinid of Lake Van, attain a maximum recorded total length of 27.8 centimeters [Li = 27.8 centimeters], a size that reflects the species' adaptation to the lake's unique alkaline-saline environment. Body mass at this ultimate size reaches approximately 202 grams [Wwi = approximately 202 grams], derived from length-weight relationships observed in local populations sampled during the spawning run. In contrast, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae first emerge from the demersal adhesive eggs at a remarkably small wet weight of just 0.0038 grams [Wwb = 0.0038 grams], a value consistent with the modest egg dimensions typical of the genus Alburnus. At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals achieve a body length of about 11 centimeters [Lp = about 11 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight of roughly 11.2 grams [Wwp = roughly 11.2 grams] at puberty. This transition from juvenile to reproductively capable adult occurs well before the attainment of maximum size, a life-history pattern common among iteroparous freshwater cyprinids that must balance growth with early reproductive investment in a seasonally pulsed environment.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], embryonated eggs of Alburnus tarichi require approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] from fertilization to the moment of chorion rupture and larval eclosion. This developmental duration is typical for cyprinids of moderate egg size incubated at this thermal regime. Following hatching, the yolk-sac larva remains in an endotrophic stage for several days before the onset of exogenous feeding, during which the mouth gape develops and prey detection capability emerges. The thermal dependence of this early life interval has direct consequences for larval survival in Lake Van's cool, alkaline waters, where spawning is timed to coincide with spring inflows that moderate salinity and provide suitable nursery habitat for the delicate prolarvae. These abiotic constraints likely contribute to the relatively constrained spawning period observed in local populations.

Field surveys indicate that Alburnus tarichi has a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under natural conditions in Lake Van, a value documented from scale-based age determinations and validated by recapture data from mark at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]ed individuals. This longevity is noteworthy for a cyprinid of its body size and suggests a relatively slow life-history pace compared to smaller, shorter-lived congeners such as Alburnus alburnus. Mortality rates increase markedly after the fifth or sixth year, coinciding with observable signs of physiological senescence and reduced condition factor. At the stable temperatures common in the lake's deeper strata during summer stratification (19 °C [T = 19 °C]), such longevities are only achievable if metabolic demands are balanced by adequate foraging opportunities on the abundant zooplankton and benthic invertebrates that constitute the primary diet of adult Tarek. Senescent individuals ultimately succumb to a combination of age-related physiological deterioration and increased vulnerability to predation.

Reproductive output in the Tarek is substantial, with gravid females producing a relatively large annual clutch when assessed under the thermal conditions typical of the spawning period at 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. During a single spawning event, each female releases approximately 110 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 110 eggs per clutch], and the majority of reproductively active individuals complete approximately 45 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 45 spawning events per year], yielding a total annual fecundity of roughly 5,000 eggs per female [Ri = annual fecundity of roughly 5,000 eggs per female]. This level of reproductive investment is consistent with the high fecundity reported for other lacustrine populations of Alburnus, where egg size and clutch frequency are shaped by the trade-off between maximizing propagule number and ensuring sufficient per-egg provisioning for survival in the challenging soda-lake environment. The synchrony of spawning with the brief spring season imposes a tight window for gamete release and fertilization.

The comparative life-history strategy of Alburnus tarichi becomes evident when examining the allometric scaling of its body weight. The pubertal mass of 11.2 grams [Wwp = 11.2 grams] represents only about 5.5 percent of the asymptotic adult mass of 202 grams [Wwi = 202 grams], indicating that a substantial fraction of post-settlement growth occurs after the onset of reproductive maturity. This protracted growth phase allows iteroparous adults to continue increasing fecundity with body size across consecutive spawning seasons. The ultimate total length of 27.8 centimeters [Li = 27.8 centimeters] places Tarek at the larger end of the size spectrum for European and West Asian Alburnus species, a trait likely linked to the high productivity and stable thermal regime of Lake Van's lacustrine ecosystem. Ongoing studies using otolith microchemistry continue to refine estimates of age-specific growth trajectories in this remarkable endemic species, which belongs to the family Cyprinidae, a group characterized by remarkable diversity in life-history strategies across freshwater habitats.
